Downeast Woodbank Penobscot, Maine LD 1525
Sen. Ross, Rep. Pluecker and honorable members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry.
My name is Anthony Aman. I am a board member of the Down East Wood Bank in Surry. I live in the
Town of Penobscot. Thank you for considering passing this legislation to promote wood banks in
Maine.
Compared to some other wood banks we are a small operation but we have a big job to do. We started
only three years ago on land generously provided by the Blue Hill Heritage Trust. With the dedicated
efforts of our small board of directors, we are now a 501c3, we built some storage buildings, we have two splitting machines, some chainsaws, and lots of wheelbarrows. Throughout the winter we met
nearly every Saturday morning, splitting, stacking, and loading cars and trucks with firewood.
We do not require our recipients to reveal their financial information or to explain why they are in
need. That is none of our business. Most often they will offer a description of their circumstances,
which sometimes are heartbreaking. We were contacted by the pastor of a local church who had just
visited an elderly couple. He noticed they were wearing outdoor clothing indoors. They said their furnace was broken and had no money to fix it.
You get to know your neighbors a little better when you are loading their pickup trucks. One young family lives in an uninsulated cabin, no refrigeration, electricity run with a generator when they
have fuel. Both adults are employed but earn barely enough to make ends meet. We are their lifeline
during winter months.
During the 2022-2023 heating season we gave away about 18 cords of wood. This past season, about
104 cords. We hope to double that amount for next heating season.
I am sure you are aware of the recent cuts the Feds imposed on_the LIHEAP program. We are expecting the demand for firewood will only increase as a result of this short-sighted decision. We also
expect more people will begin using firewood who might not be aware of the safety considerations such as installing smoke detectors and cleaning the chimney regularly. Expect more news reports of chimney fires, and asphyxiations in the coming years. The net result is not cost savings but more
strain on our fire departments and emergency services, and of course lives lost.
This bill will be a great boost to our work. The population of the towns we serve is about 17,000. This
winter we served 208 families. We cannot possibly fill the increasing need without more neighboring
towns establishing woodbanks. And we are here to help do that by providing start-up assistance and advice. It is in everybody's self interest to pass this legislation. Thank you.
10044638:
Benjamin West New Vineyard LD 1525
Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker and members of the ACF Committee. My name is Benjamin West. I am a resident of New Vineyard and while I am submitting comments 'neither for nor against' LD 1525, I thought I would list the problems with the heating assistance program as I see it now, and what I would like to see for a more effective program going forward. I'll try to keep this brief.
The Negative:
- I think it should be obvious by now that allowing people on assistance receive checks for the wood directly and then go out and purchase the wood themselves just leaves patrons of the program buying other products. The local firewood company that has delivered to the program for many many years said he saw a 90% or more reduction of the people he delivered to every year on the program ordering wood. They were spending the money on other things.
-The program (in some instances) currently is administered by people that simply call the same firewood guy for almost all of the deliveries and then go to the other distributors when their personal favorite (friend or family possibly) firewood person is unavailable. They will say that the firewood company they keep calling is the only one that will deliver on the program, but it is simply not true.
-The program should ideally encourage people to get their firewood earlier in the season when the wood can be green and season as they get closer to winter. Most people on the program are getting green wood that does not burn as efficiently because they are ordering it in the winter time. Seasoned wood ordered in the winter sells at a premium. Tax payer programs should try to avoid this premium.
Things to know:
-Not all firewood is the same. Program should ensure that nobody is delivering loads with softwood mixed in. People that deliver should be told that only hardwood is allowed on the program.
-The people ordering the wood should be given options for who to purchase through, because they'll choose the best firewood if given the option. Or they will choose the most they can purchase with the allowance they are given.
-Not all delivery locations are the same. Some driveways are very hazardous to deliver to, or are not plowed and cleared off well enough to deliver. This is why a flat rate delivery option where every cord has the same price is difficult to offer.
My Suggestions:
-For the reasons listed above, and maybe for some I've forgotten to list, the following is my suggestion for how the program should be administered. Orders should be encouraged as early as possible in the season for the benefit of the firewood contractors who inevitably get busy in the late fall and winter, so the customers will get the best pricing and have time for the wood to season. When the program has a firewood order to purchase, they should email or call the firewood companies that sign up to be on an order list and give them 24 hours to respond with their best price to deliver that load of wood. Or alternatively how much wood they will deliver/sell for the budget of the customer. This will ensure that the firewood is delivered at a good price for the customer as well as the taxpayers, and it gives the firewood company time to check out the delivery customer's delivery situation to make sure they are comfortable with their ability to deliver wood to the customer given the delivery location.
In my mind it's ludicrous to think of the amount of money that is spent by simply giving firewood orders to the same account again and again, with no bid process for the expenditure of tax dollars. Finally, the payments for the program should be administered quickly and regularly, without a lot of paperwork to complete to receive

payment. Firewood distributors on the whole are a paperwork-adverse group of people, and will put a surcharge on wood they have to wait a while or fill out paperwork to get paid for. Let's not complicate something that's very simple.
That's my opinion. If anyone has any follow up questions please feel free to call me at 207-491-7470.
Sincerely,
Benjamin West

Brittany Gill CHIP, inc LD 1525
Dear members of the Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry Committee,
Thank you for your service. I am writing in support of LD 1525, An Act to Promote Firewood Banks in Maine.
I work for CHIP a small non profit in Lincoln County. As one of our services, we provide households that are not able to meet their heating needs with a small boost for the winter: their choice of 100 gallons of K-1, #2 fuel oil, a ton of wood pellets, or electrical equivalent. Thanks to generous volunteers in our area, we are also able to offer 1 cord of wood.
The wood comes from neighbors who have had a tree fall during a storm or maybe donate wood from a clearing for a development. The requests this year were the highest they have been in the last 9 years that I have been working with CHIP. 375 unique households requested help with fuel. 45 of those households chose firewood.
Our lead organizer is gathering donations this spring and summer to cut this fall and winter for the 26-27 season. We already have 50 cords drying for 25-26 winter. The volunteers work hard to make a real difference in people's lives. Often the delivery comes and someone rushes in a few pieces of wood to start the fire.
With the support of this bill, hopefully, more people will learn about the wood banks, enabling more donations of wood and sharing knowledge. I am grateful for any protection of the good work of the volunteers.
I hope Li-Heap programs, including CAP agencies and Maine Housing, would also be purposefully made aware of these programs.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Warmly, Brittany Gill Program Manager, CHIP inc www.chipinc.org

The Cumberland Wood Bank started with a neighbor, who was a new widow, with no furnace or
firewood for her wood stove, started burning her furniture.
Later, a young mother with 3 young children was burning the kitchen cabinet doors to keep her pipes from freezing. Both were residents in one of the wealthiest towns of Maine.

A wood bank has 4 key functions:

. Dry or season it to 20% moisture content or less. deliver the wood with volunteers' trucks and trailers
Efficiency requires expensive equipment, safety training, and dedicated volunteers. In less than 2
years of operation we will do over 100 cords of donated hardwood with over 50 volunteers. In
Cumberland, it took 7 years to achieve 100 cords/year
We are supporting LD 1525 because we are trying to make it lower cost, faster, and easier to start
new wood banks across the state.

Testimony of
DANA A. DORAN
Executive Director Professional Logging Contractors of the Northeast
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry
on LD 1525, An Act to Promote Firewood Banks in Maine
Thursday, April 17, 2025
Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and members of the Joint Standing Committee
on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry, my name is Dana Doran, and I am the Executive
Director of the Professional Logging Contractors of the Northeast (PLC). The PLC is a regional
non-profit educational organization that educates the public on professional logging and trucking issues throughout the Northeast, predominately in the state of Maine.
As background, the PLC was created in 1995 to give logging and associated trucking contractors
a voice in a rapidly changing forest products industry. As of 2021, logging and trucking contractors in Maine employed over 3,000 people directly and were indirectly responsible for the creation of an additional 2,500 jobs. This employment and the investments that contractors make contributed $582 million to the state's economy. Our membership, which includes over 220 contractor members in the state of Maine and an additional 125 associate members, is
responsible for more than 80% of Maine's annual timber harvest.
Thank you for the opportunity to testify on behalf of our members in support of LD 1525, An Act
to Promote Firewood Banks in Maine. We appreciate Representative Ray for introducing this
legislation, which highlights the important role that wood heat plays in Maine's economy. Wood
has consistently proven to be a reliable and locally sourced heating option, especially in a state
like ours.
LD 1525 promotes the success of local firewood banks in rural communities by directing the Bureau to develop and distribute informational resources about effective wood bank operations. Encouraging the use of wood banks has multiple benefits. By increasing access to affordable
heat it supports our neighbors in need and local communities in rural Maine. It also inspires
philanthropic donations which is the very fabric of this state. Many of our contractor members already donate to local wood banks as a way to give back and this bill creates a framework to
support those efforts.
Maine is colder, more rural and unfortunately has some of the poorest counties in the country. It also has a long-standing tradition of using wood as a primary heat source. During the winter

months, many residents face difficulty heating their homes and must turn to fuel assistance programs. Instead of having to apply through a government program that is subject to the whim and mercy of Congress each year to receive heating assistance, the wood banks offer an
alternative that is practical, sustainable, and a glowing example of Maine's heritage and community centric philanthropy.
Wood is a renewable natural resource that is readily available in our state. The dollars spent on
it remain in the local economy, supporting Maine jobs and communities rather than flowing out of state or overseas. Responsible local harvesting of this resource also reduces our reliance on fossil fuels and contributes to climate resilience.
At a time when there is increasing pressure to electrify everything and invest heavily in alternative energy sources, LD 1525 offers a cost-effective solution inspired by tradition and community. It recognizes the value of wood heat in Maine and the unique role firewood banks
can play in meeting that need.
Thank you for your time and consideration. I respectfully urge you to vote Ought to Pass on LD 1525 and I would be happy to answer any questions you may have.

DATE: 4/17/2025 TO: Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry FROM: Darian Dyer, Deputy Director, Alliance for Green Heat, darian@forgreenheat.org
RE: Public Hearing on LD 1525, An Act to Promote Firewood Banks in Maine
Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation & Forestry:
My name is Darian Dyer and I'm the Deputy Director of Alliance for Green Heat, a national nonprofit working to promote cleaner burning residential wood heat. I'm here today to offer testimony in support of LD 1525, An Act to Promote Firewood Banks in Maine. I'd first like to thank Representative Ray for sponsoring this legislative document and the many co-sponsors that support this effort. Maine is well known for their firewood bank organizations, so it's an honor to be here to speak to the work that they do and vocalize why the State of Maine should formally support that work.
Since the Fall of 2022, the Alliance for Green Heat has been operating the Firewood Bank Assistance Program, in coordination with the U.S. Forest Service, to provide educational resources and small grants to firewood banks across the country. The goal was to help aid existing and start-up wood banks and support the practical use of non-marketable wood in communities by giving wood waste a higher purpose. When the program was launched, we only knew of about 65 firewood banks and after three years we now know there are over 150. We've worked closely with 11 firewood banks in the state of Maine that serve the counties of Cumberland, Sagadahoc, Lincoln, Waldo, Hancock, and Washington.
I cannot say strongly enough how much impact these groups have had in reducing energy poverty. While each wood bank may look or run a little differently, they all fill a critical need in each of their communities: keeping their neighbors warm when options are severely limited. For some, a delivery of firewood from a wood bank means that they'll be able to afford their prescription medication that month or groceries that week. Firewood banks also work diligently to deliver seasoned wood to homes, reducing the likelihood that unseasoned wood would be resorted to in desperate circumstances, reducing smoke and creating better health outcomes for the home and the community.
Maine wood banks have told us that the need is greater than what they can serve. LD 1525 would support existing firewood banks and shine a spotlight on their practical, community-based approach to delivering emergency fuel. With the state's active support of wood banks, we believe this will increase volunteer numbers, heighten fundraising abilities for the programs, and inspire more action on the municipal level.
6909 Laurel Ave #5461 | Takoma Park, Maryland 20912 | 301-204-9562 contact@forgreenheat.org | www.forgreenheat.org

In conclusion, the collaboration seen in LD 1525 between firewood banks, University of Maine, the Maine Forest Service, as well as involving municipalities, marks a promising direction in creating a stronger network to address wood heating needs within the state. During a time when funding for energy assistance seems to be on the chopping block for many, the support for firewood banks is more important than ever. We strongly support LD 1525 both for what it could mean for those struggling to heat their homes and for firewood banks working to provide assistance. Thank you, Darian Dyer

Testimony on LD 1525, An Act to Promote Firewood Banks in Maine

Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Piueoker, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation & Forestry:
My name is Jessica Leahy and l am a professor in the School of Forest Resources at
the University of Maine. This public flagship university is Maine's only R1 research
university and a national leader in forest education, research, and innovation. We are
providing written testimony to inform your consideration of LD 1525, An Act to Promote Firewood Banks in Maine, as amended by the sponsor. Specifically, we would like to highlight that UMaine is here as a resource and partner for wood bank initiatives.
UMaine has conducted research and provided outreach to wood banks for over a decade. Students and faculty became interested in the use of one of our most abundant
renewable resources in Maine -- our forests -- to address the significant heating
insecurity issues in our rural communities. In a recent summary of 211 inquiries, the number of calls for heating assistance were three times the number of calls about food pantries (12,000 calls vs. 4,000 calls between July 2023 and June 2024).
UMaine's research was influential in the development of language included in the federal Bipartisan Infrastructure Law that led to a short-term program focused on expanding capacity and starting new wood banks across the United States. Over the last three years, 130 wood banks have received funding ranging from $3,500 for start up wood banks to $15,000 for established wood banks. This was one-time funding for all wood banks distributing less than 100 cords. Maine led the nation in having the most
wood banks supported by this funding source. When we began our study of wood banks in 2014, we identified three wood banks in the state of Maine. Now there are 12 wood banks, including the newest one in Wade, the first that we are aware of in Aroostook
County.
The areas that would benefit most from a local wood bank are those with both a high
percentage of households with high housing cost burden and a high percentage of
households that heat primarily with wood. We calculated demand for wood banks based
on data from the American Community Survey and 63 communities in Maine had

significant potential demand for a wood bank. This is far more communities than the current 12 wood banks can serve. Links to this research are below.
One thing we have consistently heard from our local wood bank partners is that their
primary barriers were knowing about wood banks as a solution to needs in their community and then, figuring out how to get started. LD 1525 provides opportunities for potential leaders and volunteers to learn more about wood banks, and to connect wood
banks with one another. Wood banks would benefit from learning more about managing
forests for firewood objectives, considerations to prevent the spread of forest pests and diseases, and safe burning practices.
LD 1525 represents a step toward addressing increasing awareness of and resources for wood banks across Maine. UMaine looks fon/vard to continuing to be a resource and partner to the State and others as we move fon/vard with local, renewable solutions to keeping Mainers warm through the winter.

Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and esteemed members of the Joint Standing
Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry, my name is Melanie Sachs, and I am honored to represent the community of Freeport in the Maine Legislature. I am before you today
to express my strong support of LD 1525, An Act to Promote Firewood Banks in Maine.
On December 14, 2023, my constituent Tony Dimarco sent an email to me, which began "Hi
Melanie- It's your neighbor. . .. I have an interest in creating a wood bank to provide heating assistance for the residents of Freeport (likely Durham and Pownal) and I was hoping to get some advice from you..."
I connected him that day with the newly formed (at the time) wood bank in Cmnberland, and they were off. One year later ----~ after securing operating space, obtaining grant money for
equipment, building a website, making connections with our local social service provider for
referrals, recruiting volunteers, receiving and preparing donated wood and many, many long
hours -- the Freeport Wood Bank was up and rumiing, spreading warmth and connecting
community, one neighbor at a time.
LD 1525 takes this informal process and provides critical support to make it easier for other
Maine towns to start a wood bank in their own communities.
This is not just a feel-good community initiative. The handful of community wood banks in our
state fill a critical need. The Maine Home Energy Burden Study released in December 2024 indicates that 50% of Maine households use firewood for some heat source, with 10% using it exclusively. Low-income households in Maine are facing total energy burdens of 30% of
household income. This burden includes spending on electricity, household fuels and
transportation energy, and is triple the total energy burden faced by all Maine households. As the
House chair of the Legislative Energy, Utilities and Technology Committee, I am acutely aware
of the many factors that are influencing total energy burden, and the efforts to reduce that burden on all Mainers, particularly those who have lower incomes.

District 102: Freeport

I am also aware of the impact this assistance has on those who receive it. I have been a licensed
clinical social worker for 30 years and was the Executive Director of Freeport Community
Services (FCS), arranging for fuel assistance for those in my community, including wood. I know how this critical support helps the most vulnerable in our community. That load of wood
can be the difference between staying warm or struggling in a cold home. On the Freepoit Wood Bank's website, they note their mission is "grounded in community spirit and mutual care," coming together "to make sure everyone stays warm during Maine's cold months." The need is great, and the time is now. I urge the committee to come together and vote
to support this growing network of organizations.

Sec. 2. 38 MRSA �342, sub-�18 is enacted to read:
18. Guidance to firewood banks. The commissioner shall provide guidance to municipalities or counties in this State operating firewood banks concerning management of enviromnental impacts and solid-waste disposal associated with the operation of a firewood bank. For the purposes of this subsection, "firewood bank" has the same meaning as in Title 12, section 9731,
subsection 1.
SUMMARY
The bill defines "firewood bank" as an organization that accepts donations of firewood and makes firewood available free of charge to individuals and families in need of heating assistance.
This amendment clarifies that a firewood bank may also purchase firewood for the same
purpose.
The amendment strikes from the bill the requirement that any time there are timber or forest harvesting operations on state-owned land located within 50 miles of a firewood bank, the State is required to offer a donation of 8 to l3 cords of hardwood to that firewood bank.
The amendment also strikes from the bill the provision that clarifies that a firewood bank and the municipality or county in which a firewood bank is located is not liable for any damages caused by the taking or use of firewood obtained from a firewood bank.
The amendment changes references to the University of Maine Cooperative Extension Service to the University of Maine System.

Good afternoon Senator Talbot-Ross, Representative Pluecker, and honorable members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry. Thank you for the opportunity to submit testimony on the behalf of LD 1525. My name is Tony DiMarco and l live in
Freeport. l represent the Freeport Wood Bank and l am also a co-founder of the Maine Wood Banks Network. The Freeport Wood Bank is one of the newest wood banks in the state, and we
operate on an acre of land at the Freeport Recycling Center that was generously granted to us
by the town of Freeport.
Every Saturday we host a small crew of volunteers who work hard to haul logs, split
them, and then stack the firewood. These are community building events, as volunteers can see the tangible results of their labor and the positive impact that this firewood will have on
households in our community. ln the fall and throughout the winter we deliver the firewood to
people in need. As you've heard, their circumstances are often desperate, but their gratitude is resounding and rewarding.
Heating with firewood is a tradition and a part of people's quality of life. There are actions
people can take to burn wood safely and efficiently. Wood is plentiful, it's renewable, and we
make it available. For many Mainers, receiving free wood is their best option for staying warm. I urge you to support this bill because of its focus on wood bank awareness which is
generally lacking throughout the state, even in towns like Freeport where wood banks exist. The
bill also creates a foundation for what can be a critical resource for our communities. it will help
us generate donations of wood and funding, and it will help us recruit volunteers. And perhaps most importantly it will motivate more communities to start their own wood banks.
At the same time, l can tell you that the barriers to entry for wood banks can be high
because of the costs of equipment, insurance, and supplies, and there are no longer any
targeted sources of funding for wood bank startups. Unfortunately this financial barrier can be insurmountable for some groups who are interested in starting a wood bank in their community. So while l believe this bill is an important step, l also think it is just a first step in creating a broad and sustainable network of wood banks in our state.
I mentioned at the start of my comments that I am a co-founder of the Maine Wood
Banks Network. lt is a state-wide organization that sen/es as the non-profit sponsor for Freeport
Wood Bank, and has proven to be invaluable as a general resource for expertise and shared
equipment. You will hear more about that next. Thank you for the hard work that you do in support of the people of Maine. l hope that
you will support this important bill.
